blocks.text: Quick verdict

Decodo is the better choice for most scraping teams: its 115M+ pool is roughly three times Infatica's, it is cheaper at both 10 GB ($35 against $40) and 100 GB ($275 against $360), and its benchmark success rates are near perfect. Infatica is the better pick when you need IPv6 residential IPs, when procurement wants ISO certifications and a written no-reselling policy, or when you want a cheap week-long trial before committing. On features alone, the two are closer than the price gap suggests.

Decodo and Infatica are both well-regarded mid-market residential providers with similar entry prices around $4/GB. Decodo brings a much larger pool, polished self-service and a family of scraping APIs. Infatica brings ZIP targeting on every plan, a $4 seven-day trial, an IPv6 residential pool and a strong ethical-sourcing position. This comparison looks at where each one's advantages actually change the outcome for scraping, SERP, e-commerce and compliance-sensitive teams.

blocks.text: Decodo in 2026: what you get

Decodo is the 2024 rebrand of Smartproxy, one of the most popular mid-market providers. Its residential network is advertised at 115 million IPs across 195+ locations, and independent benchmarks put its success rate around 99.9% with sub-second response times. Every plan includes the full pool plus city, state, ZIP and ASN targeting, and the dashboard is one of the easiest to set up. Decodo also sells datacenter, ISP and mobile proxies and a family of scraping APIs.

Strengths: Large 115M+ pool at a mid-market price; Near-perfect success rates in independent tests; Clean, fast self-service onboarding; Scraping APIs available when raw proxies are not enough. Weak spots: Plan traffic does not roll over; Published pricing stops at 100 GB; beyond that you need a quote; More expensive per GB than budget brands.
Infatica in 2026: what you get

Infatica is a web-data provider with offices in the UK, Singapore and the UAE. It started with premium residential proxies and now sells mobile, static ISP, datacenter and IPv6 residential networks plus scraper APIs and datasets. Its residential pool is advertised at 35M-40M IPs in 195 countries, with ZIP-level targeting on every plan, and the company is unusually explicit about sourcing: it says it does not resell IPs and lists several ISO certifications.

Strengths: ZIP targeting included on every plan; Clear sourcing policy and ISO certifications; Cheap 7-day trial; Rare IPv6 residential pool. Weak spots: Mid-range pool size; Per-GB price stays above $3.50 until large volumes; Subscription traffic does not roll over.
Pricing: Decodo vs Infatica

Decodo sells residential traffic at $4/GB pay-as-you-go with no commitment, or on monthly plans: 3 GB for $11.25 ($3.75/GB), 10 GB for $35, 25 GB at $3.25/GB, 50 GB for $150 and 100 GB for $275 ($2.75/GB). Top-ups are billed at your plan's rate, so you are not pushed into the next tier.

Infatica charges $4/GB pay-as-you-go for residential traffic. Subscriptions cost $3.84/GB at 25 GB, $3.60/GB at 100 GB, and fall to about $2.70/GB at 500 GB and $2.60/GB at 1 TB. Premium IPv6 residential runs at roughly 1.5x those rates, starting at $6/GB.

At 10 GB a month, Decodo is the cheaper option at about $35 against $40 for Infatica, roughly 12% less. For a 100 GB month, Decodo costs about $275 while Infatica costs about $360, so Decodo saves around 24%. Both Decodo and Infatica work on allowances that do not carry forward indefinitely, so size your plan to real monthly usage rather than buying ahead.
Pool size, coverage and targeting

By advertised size, Decodo (115M+) is about 3.3x larger than Infatica (35M-40M). Advertised pool sizes are marketing figures counted over long periods; the number of IPs actually reachable in a given country at a given moment is far smaller for every provider, so treat these as a rough guide to depth rather than a guarantee. For coverage, Decodo lists 195+ countries and Infatica lists 195. On targeting, Decodo offers country, state, city, ZIP and ASN, while Infatica offers country, state, city and ZIP.
Protocols, sessions and setup

Both providers support SOCKS5 as well as HTTP(S), so either will plug into scrapers, anti-detect browsers and automation tools that expect a SOCKS endpoint. On sessions, Decodo offers rotating or sticky sessions with configurable duration, and Infatica offers per-request rotation or selectable rotation times. Setup works the same way on both: a single gateway endpoint, with location and session options passed as username parameters, plus IP whitelisting if you prefer not to use credentials.
Which is better for your use case?

General web scraping: Decodo wins. The deciding factor for Decodo: a large pool and near-perfect benchmark success rates. The limitation on the Infatica side: fast proxies that did well on popular targets in independent tests.

SERP and rank tracking: tie. Neither has a clear edge. With Decodo: a dedicated SERP scraping API plus city targeting. With Infatica: ZIP targeting helps local search results. Run the same small test on both before committing.

Social media and multi-account management: Decodo wins. The deciding factor for Decodo: sticky sessions, sub-users and an easy dashboard. The limitation on the Infatica side: rotation controls are good but very long sticky sessions are not a headline feature.

E-commerce price and stock monitoring: tie. Neither has a clear edge. With Decodo: ZIP targeting and a ready-made e-commerce API. With Infatica: ZIP-level targeting for local prices. Run the same small test on both before committing.

Ad verification and geo-testing: tie. Neither has a clear edge. With Decodo: wide coverage with city and ASN targeting. With Infatica: precise geo targeting and clean sourcing. Run the same small test on both before committing.

Tight budgets: tie. Neither has a clear edge. With Decodo: it is mid-priced, not cheap. With Infatica: mid-range pricing until you reach large volumes. Run the same small test on both before committing.
Trials, verification and billing fine print

Before you pay, check how each provider lets you test. Decodo: Free trial (about 100 MB) on residential. Infatica: 7-day trial for $4 (residential) or $8 (mobile). Verification and payment rules differ too. Decodo: Light KYC; checks on some targets. Infatica: Standard verification; states it does not resell IPs. Whichever you choose, measure cost per successful request rather than cost per gigabyte: retries, blocked pages and heavy page assets all burn bandwidth, and a cheaper network that fails more often can end up costing more. Blocking images and fonts in your scraper, reusing sessions where a target allows it, and capping concurrency are the quickest ways to cut the bill on either provider.
How to test Decodo and Infatica before you commit
Spec sheets only get you so far. A short, structured test on your own targets will settle Decodo vs Infatica faster than any review:
1. Buy the smallest option on each side (Decodo: free trial (about 100 MB) on residential; Infatica: 7-day trial for $4 (residential) or $8 (mobile)).
2. Pick three to five real target URLs and the two or three countries that matter most, and send the same number of requests (a few hundred is enough) through each provider at the same time of day.
3. Record success rate, median response time, CAPTCHAs or blocks, and the number of unique exit IPs you received per country.
4. Divide what you spent by the number of successful, correctly located responses to get cost per useful request, then scale that to your monthly volume.
Bottom line

Across the six use cases above, Decodo comes out ahead in 2, Infatica in 0, and 4 are ties. That makes Decodo the safer default if you are unsure, but the right answer still depends on your volume and targets: Decodo is strongest for small and mid-size scraping teams, while Infatica is strongest for compliance-conscious buyers. If you can, spend a few dollars testing both on the exact sites and countries you care about; a one-hour test tells you more than any spec sheet.

Developers who want enterprise-like quality without contracts
Mixed workloads that may grow into scraping APIs
Infatica is the better pick for:

Location-precise collection that needs ZIP targeting
Teams wanting IPv6 residential IPs
